As far as the Scene Tracker goes, I definitely see the value in it between both keeping the scene from going too long and being so tied in to the game's mechanics of allowing more extreme abilities and threats as the situation gets more dire.  But it also seems like it could definitely be a bit too constricting and will also likely be unbalanced for certain player counts.  A compromise I've thought of is to still have the scene escalate through GYRO, but not have a Scene Tracker actually visible to the players.  All they would know is what color the scene currently is.  The GM could still be using their own hidden Scene Tracker, or they could just be using their judgment on when to switch zones.  Either way would allow them to adjust to fit how the group is doing so they can keep the tension high, but not just make things impossible.  This also seems to make more sense thematically, because unless there's a bomb counting down or something, the heroes usually wouldn't know exactly how much time they have before things get really bad.  They shouldn't be going into a situation thinking "Ok team, we've got exactly 8 rounds to neutralize this threat."

I feel like this may have gotten lost amongst all the other comments, so what do people think about my idea of not letting the players see the scene tracker?

PlatinumWarlock wrote:
In one Action scene, one character may be overwatching a hallway with a pulse cannon, while another hacks the high-security lock, and a third works to cobble together a makeshift explosive.  
Yeah, and it's like:1. You have to figure out that hacking a security lock is what needs to be done in the first place. (Step 1)2. You have to get together the materials to handle this. (Step 2)3. You have to actually do it. (Step 3)4. If it fails, you have to either repeat this all over again or come up with a Plan B.This is totally fine in RP that's allowed to progress at a normal state of speed. That's not fine when you've got only a limited amount of turns to do things.Same more or less with the explosive. Figuring out what you want to do. Getting together what you need to do it. Accounting for what happens if it doesn't work the first time.

Okay. Let's break this down in Sentinels RPG terms during an action scene:

1. Figure out hacking the lock - This is done for you as the gamemaster sets up the scene, and if using the index card element, then there's "Objective: Hack the Security Lock!" put out in front of the players.

  1. Get together materials to do it - This is where I think you might have been lead astray. At the session at Gen Con, Phillipe-Antoine explained that you are a superhero and have all your superhero tricks already on you, within reason. While Wraith might not be carrying a supercomputer around, she does have her wrist computer that is wirelessly hooked up to her supercomputer within her lair, and if the player doesn't think of that, then the gamemaster can say, you know, you do have your gadgets on you, can you think of one that might help here? Then the player says yeah, I whip out my mini calculator computer and hook into the system! Boom! Done! The materials you need are already on you by virtue of you being a superhero. Wraith would NEVER go anywhere without her gadgets, and since it is a comic book atmosphere any needed tech or materials can be explained away using comic book logic. In another RPG, sure, there could be a whole session dedicated to getting the specific tech you need to do the job, but this is comic book world. The readers don't need all that prep!

  2. Do it! - Yeah, well, this step tends to be what happens in the Sentinels RPG. First, the player describes what they're doing ("I'm going to hack into the security lock using my wrist computer!"), then they do it (assembles a dice pool from their stats that fits hacking into the security lock with their wrist computer).

  3. If it fails, repeat or do something else - Well, ya. That's the idea. But there are also other techie types on the team who might be standing by to take over. Unity uses her tech skills to hack the lock when Wraith's own programming algorithms fail! The game doesn't exist in a vacuum, so realistically the entire thing is over and done with in one round, even if one player doesn't make the roll. And even if they all don't get the hack roll right, then one round goes by and the team tries again. It's no big deal, especially since the scene tracker seems to give you WAY MORE rounds than a team of heroes would ever need to complete the objectives.

Maybe you don't give your players enough credit that they can do things well even if they are under a clock. That spurs more intelligent approaches, the "fight smarter not harder!" strategies.

Why, though? Your job as GM is not to command the players to march to your beat against their will, it's to help them have fun and tell fun stories. I mean, the Sentinels RPG's own gameplay guide says this.

But it is your job as a gamemaster to make sure everyone's time is respected and valued. People take time out of their lives to get together and play games and socialize. That time is valuable and these people have made a conscious choice to sit down at your table, expecting to have a good time. One player wants to do long role-play sessions where no dice get rolled, another player had a terrible day and needs to let off some steam by punching bad guys, another player has to be out of there by a specific time because that's when the babysitter has to go home, another player has to be up in the morning and can't play past X time, another player has homework that needs to be done but they decided they would take the risk of failing an assignment because they want/need to relax with friends, and you have come in with a great adventure that has what you think are some really cool encounters and want to see everyone get through it tonight because you'll be out of town for the next month on business and want to assemble the next part of the campaign during that time.

This isn't about forcing players to march to your beat against their will. It's about making sure the game is worth everyone's time, including your own as a gamemaster. I think this is a bit over the line here, drawing conclusions based on a very narrow view of the whole picture. There's role-playing, and there's sitting there lost in analysis paralysis trying to think of what would be the "right" thing to do. Most RPGs have an in-game "window of opportunity" for the player during a combat that is typically somewhere between 3 and 6 seconds. If you are role-playing to where everything you say is in-character, then it isn't unreasonable to allow that length of time be the limit. Plus, people can talk while doing other things. Comic book heroes and villains have all kinds of witty banter while in the middle of a fight. Talking is fine. But if you're going to break down every step of every action into a series of logical steps that can only be taken one at a time, each on a different round, then I think you might be missing the point of what a comic book story involves. Here in Sentinels RPG, you can describe what your hero is doing over two or three panels in the comic book, which means condensing things down to what really matters for purposes of a comic book medium. We don't need to see Wraith look at the security lock, decide she needs to go back to her lair, go into her gadgetorium closet, select all the hack tools, lock up the gadgetorium closet, swing back through the city, approach the lock, hook up the equipment, hack the system (player actually rolls here), and then see the results. Wraith already has the gadgets she needs because she's a superhero and that's what superheroes do–they plan ahead and bring the equipment they think they'll need for any given situations. It's unreasonable to think Wraith wouldn't have that tech on her already, so why not stop wasting all that time describing Wraith going back home and back out and instead just have her whip out her gadgets and hack the dang security lock already!

Now, that being said, at Gen Con it turned out that Absolute Zero ended up on the other side of town and instead of doing something superheroic to get to the tree, he chose to take the city bus. This became hilarious, and every time it got to AZ's turn, he'd describe how he's on the bus, taking selfies with the other riders or enduring the disapproving stare of the little old lady with her bag of groceries. This was so entertaining that Phillipe-Antoine gave him a persistant bonus to set up for when AZ arrived at the tree near the end of the battle and blast the Mothership to freezing bits as he stepped off the bus.

Roleplaying can work under a clock. It's about facilitating those choices within the context of the scene and making sure everyone has a chance to do something, and some of the best roleplaying can come out of those moments of stress. I understand not wanting to feel stressed out by the game and how it could make the experience unfun. But that didn't happen at that table at Gen Con, and it doesn't happen at my tables for other games when a clock comes into play. More than anything it has gotten the players to sit up, on the edge of their seats, and focused on the game while role-playing the entire time.

One thing to keep reminding your players if they feel under pressure from the scene tracker, is that they can use an overcome to prevent it advancing in the scene's turn, of course a critical fail (0 or less) could result in it advancing further.

What I believe the reason for the scene tracker is, is that heroes are constantly working under pressure, something is about to collapse, they're threatening to kill the hostages, Baron Blade's Terra-Luna Impusion device is getting ready to be fired, ect. ect.

So in the scenes green zone you've just arrived on the scene and are still taking things in before realising how bad things are.

The Yellow is the majority of the actual conflict, the pressure is on and you're attempting to resolve things before it gets worse.

In Red things are really bad, the building is groaning really loudly and the supports holding it up are starting to snap, the hostage taker is aiming his weapon at the hostages, the firing sequence for the Terra-Luna Impulsion Device has starting counting down to the actual firing time and it's time to pull out all the stops.

This serves two purposes,

1. It gives the players a representation of how bad things are getting adding an element of tension for the players.

2. I means that when the chips are down, people are not being hamstrung by taking too little damage to help effectively if the abilities they need are in the red or yellow zone.

I guess it's that I'm used to dealing with Magic Countdown - TV Tropes

Any kind of stated time limit or countdown in fiction seems to know when it's Being Watched , and will cheat accordingly for maximum drama. This phenomenon tends to occur especially as a countdown starts approaching zero.
So I feel like from this point of view the idea of any system should be to to give the appearance of pressure to the characters in the developed plot without there being actual pressure to the players in real life.

Unless, of course, the players themselves speed things up. They decide they should be cutting wires when it actually involved turning the knobs. They crit fail their attempt at an important action. They actually go ahead and let that murderous minion finish moving logically combat turn by combat turn towards the hapless civilians without doing anything at all to try to stop them. They decide that going "Sure, go ahead, push that red button, see if we care" to the villain is a good idea. In that case, yep, go ahead and let the player have the plot-driving consequences of their actions making the condition of the scene worse.

Edit: And I guess therefore ironically what I'm saying is that I think the Minor/Major Twist system is totally perfect and would rather instead expand further on that dynamic. Because that helps things work more the way I feel comfortable with: The players themselves add bad scene-worsening elements if they pick bad/risky actions or happen to fail their rolls for things.

Jeysie, I don't know how many times I can say things along the line of "Your group may be different than mine; that's great if it is", without you coming back after me, claiming I'm attacking you, especially after I spent most of the last extended, argumentative thread agreeing with you...

I've run games for literally 25+ years.  I've run for home groups around my dining room table, I've run for groups at the biggest conventions in the US.  I've written for a number of massive companies, as well as a number of one-man-army shops on DriveThru.  I've written and published my own superheroes game, for Legacy's sake.  If you don't want to be at my table, that's fine--I've got players waiting in the wings.  But, could you at least possibly admit that what's going on at your table wouldn't always fly with people elsewhere?

If I sat down with 6-7 random people at a convention game, with an advertisement of "Omnitron returns to Megalopolis!  The Freedom Five must destroy the robotic menace before Freedom Tower falls forever!", and one of my players sat around on the bus, while the others tried to actively engage the plot, there's an active problem at the table.  One of the players is literally dragging down the rest of the group for his own, personal fun, while the others are likely struggling (or, at least, not at their optimal strength and flexibility) without his active presence.  At a table setting, it also means that the GM has to sacrifice time and effort to mollify that player, while running "the main plot" with the rest of the group.  I'm all for splitting the party...when it's in the interest in the party as a whole (i.e. "Unity, you and Wraith go that way and take out the reactor core; Tachyon, you and Bunker clear those drones.  AZ, you're with me:  let's crack that mothership's hull!").  When it's in the selfish intersest of one player?  That actively drags down the fun for everyone else at the table.  In a four hour convention game, if a full hour was devoted to one player faffing around on a city bus instead of fighting the giant robot, when the game was advertised as "Fight a giant robot!", I'd be pretty mad.  I think you would, too.

Again, your mileage may vary.  In my sizable experience, I've seen the contrary to what happens at your table.

For what it's worth, I think Phillipe adjucated that encounter very well.  He didn't make a big deal of the AZ's player's behavior, he rewarded them for rejoining the group, and didn't spend an over-large amount of time with that one player, at the detraction of the group.

You seem to think--and, I'm quoting you directly here--that my opinion is one of: ugh that's so slow of you to play like that and I'd never abide that in MY games, chop chop people.

Let me tell you a little story.  The first three sessions of the game that inspired Cold Steel Wardens, I GMing for four players:  my wife, our friend Lionel (the faculty advisor of the college roleplaying guild I founded), Will Herrmann (now the owner of Journeyman Games and the creator of the Savage Worlds Wild Card Creator), and Kat Ostrander (now, Kat Lee, the line developer for Legend of the Five Rings at Fantasy Flight games).  They're among some of the best players I've ever rolled dice with.  Do you know what the first three sessions of our campaign entailed?  Will's illegal immigrant character finding a low-paying job, low-rent housing, and a way to survive that wasn't squatting on the streets.  He didn't even meet another player character--Lionel's, in fact--until the end of the first session.

I *actively like* spending time doing nothing but in character roleplaying.  They're some of my favorite sessions, across the board.  But as a group dynamic--in my, again, not insignificant, experience--when you have half the group knee deep in zombie and the other half sitting around at the tavern, there's a significant, palpable issue with both your in-character motivational dynamics and your out-of-character/at-the-table group dynamics.  And, as the GM, it's your absolute responsibility to rectify this problem.

My point throughout this argument is no more and no less than this:  in an action scene, using hard deadlines both in-character (perhaps through the GYRO scene tracker) and out of character (through visual, verbal, and other social cues) maintains and enhances the tension of that scene.  If you take away that pressure, you also remove the tension from the scene.  

A third time, if you're okay with that and your players are okay with that, then you're fine.  I will, however, disagree with your choice, as it's actively bad storytelling technique. Telling a story--which is what, as both players and GMs is what we're doing--you've got to have conflict.  Putting the brakes on that conflict slows down the pace, the intensity, and the overall impact of your storytelling ability.  If you're okay with that and your players are okay with that, then you're fine.

As an overarching game-design philosophy, Cold Steel Wardens was designed to articulate and give voice to the moral quandary found in the Iron Age of Comics.  In the heat of the moment of an action scene, bullets fly, swords swing, punches land, and blood spills.  Yes, the chance to examine that quandary exists, but not in the depth or capacity of what the SCRPG would call a montage scene or in open-roleplay.  The depth emerges when the consequences are finally revealed:  when a vigilante sees where the bullets landed or when a would-be hero arrives just a little too late.  Without that tension, the whole game easily becomes meaningless; it's not something I'd ever be willing to sacrifice.  For me, that means that when running the SCRPG, I'm going to keep the GYRO scene tracker open, visible, and oft-utilized during action scenes.  During montage or open-roleplay scenes, I won't use it.  No more, no less.

I'm going to stress one last time that, If your group differs from mine, if your game experience differs from mine, and you're all having fun, that's spectacular.  My disagreement with how you run games is not a personal attack on you, on your group, or on your fun.  It is--precisely and nothing more--than a disagreement with the advice you're providing to other, potentially rookie, GMs.  I simply believe that deadlines and tensions have a major role to play in both player and character motivation than you seem to.

Some of my advice regards this particual topic to rookie GMs is as follows:

  1. Always communicate with your players to make sure everyone at the table is on board with what kind of game everyone wants to play and what everyone wants to get out of it.

  2. Always try to make what happens in the plot follow logically from the consequences of the players' actions and choices, so that players feel as much as possible that what they do is actually a meaningful contribution. That includes having negative consequences when applicable.

  3. Make sure that players feel excited and energized, not stressed out or flustered. It's OK for characters to be rushed when the plot calls for it, but the players shouldn't feel that way IRL.

  4. Try your best to encourage the players to actually roleplay as their characters, rather than just "I swing my sword and roll Melee" the entire time.

If any of that is bad advice, I'd honestly like to know, but it's always served to make my own experiences enjoyable.

posts.name: Selganor
posts.cooked:
I just got quite a few multicolored (red, yellow, green, blue and white) index cards and I'll probably use them for three things this evening when we are running the fourth story.

1. Heroes hitpoints and abilities
One of the characters in my group is Absolute Zero and his yoyo-hp might be easier to handle if he just has a certain amount of green/yellow/red blank index cards to indicate which zone he is in.
Colored index cards can also help the players to keep track of their colored abilities (putting away those abilities that can't be used right now)

2. Scene counter
I found it problematic in the previous 3 adventures to keep track of the scene tracker when I also have to turn pages for info on the scene, minons, ...
So I will just put a small stack of cards in the middle so the players can see what the current status is and also check how much time they will have.

3. Many other uses
So far I only used red/yellow/green, but I'll probably use the blue cards for minions, objectives, ... and may even use the white cards for short compilations of the basic actions and other rules.

I'll probably compile some rules cheat sheet - or has anyone else here done somthig like that already

posts.name: aramis
posts.cooked:
Jeysie:

Well, ironically I don’t have a problem with “railroading”, in a sense, which is why I was totally bewildered and taken aback by twoeyedjack’s lecture. I’m not out to flip off the GM’s story, the goal of players should be to work with GM as much as the GM should work with the players.

It’s amazing how many players over the years I’ve encountered who refuse flat-out to follow any GM’s prepped adventure.



It’s a different playstyle, suited best to hexcrawls and rumor-mongering GM’s prepared to wing it on a moment’s notice.  It’s different, not better, not worse. Unless you try to use a heavily-linear “The route is prefigured, what matters is if we make it through the trip” type game. Which, the Starter Kit definitely is written as.

And yes, I’ve run games for that type - lots of “throw 20 hooks, then figure out which one they want to follow” - and often intentionally adding a few travel encounters the dice don’t call for in order to delay them from reaching long enough to have the week to build the dungeon.

Now, some decry the freedom of games like SC as “illusionsim” - creating a false illusion of freedom of choice… but I’ve known (and have been, from time to time) as guilty of illusionism in a hexcrawl player-driven setup. The dungeon used is written with plans for several of the hooks, so I wrote 3 or 4 in advance, each of which had small changes based upon which hook was followed, and then replaced it with a new one… giving the players the illusion that their choice was 12+ choices, when, really, it was between 4 dungeons…
